title: Maps, the comma-ok idiom and the unordered map

videos.script: Lessons 11 to 13 kept values in a row, found by their position. This lesson finds them by a name instead. {{literal}} A map holds values under keys. You write one as a literal, add to it, change it and delete from it, and its length follows along. {{nil}} Then the one way to crash with a map. A map you declared but never made can be read, and it cannot be written. You will see the panic it prints. {{missing}} Next, a question a map cannot answer on its own. Ask for a key that is not there, and you get a zero, with no complaint. A second value, called ok, tells you which zero you got. {{order}} Last, order. Run the same program twice, and the map comes out in a different order each time. That is deliberate, and printing the map hides it. By the end you can count, group and look things up by key, and walk the keys in an order you chose.
